title: bell hooks
tradition: Feminism and the ethic of love
keyWorks: Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom (1994)
Communion: The Female Search for Love (2002)
The Will to Change: Men, Masculinity, and Love (2004)
summary: bell hooks (1952–2021; born Gloria Jean Watkins) was an American writer, feminist thinker and teacher from Kentucky. She took her pen name from her great-grandmother and wrote it in lowercase so that attention would go to her ideas rather than to her person. She wrote about love, education, race, class and gender as things that touch everyone's everyday life — in clear language addressed not only to scholars.
onEmotions: For hooks, feelings are never a purely private matter: the way we feel shame, fear or love is largely learned in the family and in the culture. She called a society built on hierarchy and control a “dominator culture” and showed that it rests on fear and shame and teaches us to hide vulnerability. hooks's answer is a “love ethic.” Love, for her, is not a feeling that simply happens but an action and a choice: following M. Scott Peck, she defines it as the will to nurture growth — your own and another person's — and following Erich Fromm she names its ingredients: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge, to which she adds trust, commitment and honest communication. She considered self-love and self-esteem the starting point, and healing a shared rather than a solitary task. Where there is abuse and humiliation there is no love — but the capacity to love can be learned anew.

anxiety.text: As a girl, Gloria Watkins — the future bell hooks — grew up in Kentucky, where segregation taught Black children to stay on guard from morning till night; later she would call a society of hierarchy, competition and control “dominator culture.” In such a culture people constantly feel judged and threatened, and anxiety is an honest response to a world in which much really is unreliable. If anxiety has become the background of your life, it is not only your personal problem. The opposite of anxiety is not fearlessness but connection: trust, honest conversation, care. Anxiety eases not when we “pull ourselves together” alone, but when we stop hiding it from those we can trust. Perhaps right now your anxiety is asking not for strictness but for care — including your own.
anxiety.practice: Say one sentence out loud to someone you trust: “What's worrying me right now is…” hooks believed anxiety eases when we stop hiding it.

fear.text: Gloria Watkins took her pen name from her great-grandmother, known for her sharp and bold tongue — as if borrowing courage. Fear is an ancient and honest feeling that wants to keep you safe, and hooks knew it well. In All About Love bell hooks observed that fear is the main force holding up relations of domination: it pushes us to separate, to hide, to avoid being known. That's why she set against fear not heroism but love, understood as action. This doesn't mean being afraid is shameful. It means fear has a counterweight available even on a very small scale: one step toward someone, one honest sentence, one request for help. Fear narrows the world down to “me against everyone,” and love widens it again. You don't need to stop being afraid first in order to make a tiny move toward connection with another person.
fear.practice: Call or tell in person someone around whom you feel a little less afraid: “I feel calmer with you.” It's a small step of love toward fear.

quote.text: When we choose to love we choose to move against fear—against alienation and separation. The choice to love is a choice to connect—to find ourselves in the other.
quote.author: bell hooks

sadness.text: “I came to theory because I was hurting,” bell hooks admitted: for her, thinking began with sadness honestly acknowledged. Your sadness deserves room and time. bell hooks wrote a great deal about how our culture teaches us to hide sadness — boys and men especially, but really all of us — as if it were a sign of weakness or ingratitude. In The Will to Change she showed how costly the emotional numbness that passes for strength can be. Allowing yourself to be sad is part of loving yourself: care begins with attention to what you actually feel, not to what you are “supposed” to feel. hooks spoke of love as a practice, and one of its simplest forms is to acknowledge, “I'm sad right now,” without demanding that you fix yourself immediately. Sadness that is seen and accepted stays heavy, but it stops being lonely.
sadness.practice: Put a hand where you feel the sadness in your body and say aloud: “I see that you're sad, and I'm with you.” hooks called this kind of attention to yourself the first act of love.

grief.text: “To be loving is to be open to grief,” bell hooks wrote in the chapter on loss in All About Love. Grief is love that has nowhere left to go, and it may last as long as it lasts. She noticed that our culture hurries the bereaved — “time to move on” — and so leaves them alone with what remains unsaid. For hooks, love doesn't end with death: care, memory and gratitude continue as action — in how we speak of the one who is gone, in what we keep, in what we learned from them. She also insisted that it is better to grieve not in isolation but in community, among those who can share your tears and your stories. Grief doesn't need to be “done right” or quickly; it needs to be lived through — ideally with support.
grief.practice: Tell someone one story today about the person you lost — funny, warm, any story. hooks believed grief is better held in community, where stories are passed on.

loneliness.text: bell hooks's grandmother sewed quilts from scraps: warmth, hooks saw, is pieced together from many small parts. Loneliness truly hurts, and behind it lies a real need — to be known and needed. bell hooks believed many people in modern culture live in a state of “lovelessness” — not because something is wrong with them, but because the culture values success, consumption and independence more than connection. At the same time hooks distinguished loneliness as being abandoned from solitude as a choice. She considered the ability to be with yourself part of the art of loving: someone who can be alone with themselves comes to others not to escape but to meet them. Her answer to loneliness is not to urgently find “the one,” but to gradually grow circles of community: friends, neighbors, people with whom you can share care. Love, she wrote, doesn't live only in couples.
loneliness.practice: Send a short message to someone with whom the connection weakened but was once warm — no reason, no expectations. One more patch for the quilt.

anger.text: Killing Rage is what bell hooks called her essay collection on racism: it opens with a scene on a plane where her friend was treated unjustly and hooks herself was flooded with anger. She insisted that anger can be a healthy response to oppression rather than a flaw of character: it can be precise, noticing injustice before reason finds the words. But she also distinguished anger that helps us see and act from anger that turns into a wish to dominate another. Her “love ethic” — a life in which care, respect and justice become the main guides — doesn't ask you to suppress anger. It asks what the anger is serving: the defense of dignity or the destruction of connection. Anger that is listened to carefully often points to a value that has been hurt.
anger.practice: Say aloud — in an empty room or on a walk — one sentence your anger wants to speak, starting with “What matters to me is…” hooks called this talking back: giving anger a voice, not a fist.

shame.text: In Bone Black, her memoir of girlhood, bell hooks describes a girl who felt like a stranger in her family, “wrong” — the voice of shame, which says not “I did something bad” but “I am bad.” bell hooks wrote that shaming is a familiar tool of power: in families, schools and society people are often raised through humiliation, and the mark lasts a long time. In All About Love she recalled that in her childhood harshness and punishment were called love — and only with time did she understand that care and shaming are incompatible. For hooks, shame grows in silence and isolation and weakens when it can be spoken aloud in the presence of someone who won't judge. This doesn't mean you have to open up to everyone. But it does mean your shame is not a verdict — often it is an imprint of how you were once treated.
shame.practice: Ask yourself whose voice your shame is speaking in — and answer it aloud in one sentence, the way hooks learned to talk back to adults: “I was treated badly, but that doesn't make me a bad person.”

guilt.text: From Erich Fromm bell hooks took a simple idea: to love is to answer for how we affect those around us. So guilt, which shows you care how your actions touch others, is for her part of love. But responsibility, for her, is not endless self-punishment. Self-flagellation, as her thinking suggests, locks us up in ourselves and gets in the way of doing what really matters: acknowledging what we did, apologizing, making amends where possible. hooks valued honesty above flawlessness: anyone can make a mistake, and love is tested by what we do after it. Guilt can be turned from a burden into a step — not “what a terrible person I am,” but “what can I do now.”
guilt.practice: Do one small thing that acknowledges what happened: a short “I'm sorry,” returning something, an offer to help. hooks measured love by what we do after a mistake.

envy.text: The chapter on greed in All About Love is one of its sharpest: bell hooks shows how consumer culture trains us to measure our worth by what we have and how we look next to others. Envy, meanwhile, is unpleasant but very human, and behind it there is often a wish worth hearing. In that logic, someone else's good fortune feels like a personal loss. hooks offered a different measure — the values we live by: care, generosity, community. Envy shows not that you are a bad person but what you are missing — recognition, rest, opportunities, love. If you translate envy into a question about your own needs, it stops being poison and becomes a clue.
envy.practice: Imagine envy is a letter from one of your needs, written in clumsy handwriting. Read it to yourself: what is it really asking for — rest, recognition, love?

emptiness.text: A cup can only hold what is poured into it — this is how bell hooks thought about “lovelessness,” the quiet epidemic of our time: many grew up without reliable care and later try to fill the lack with things, work, other people's approval. Emptiness is a strange feeling, as if there were nothing inside to hold on to. This is not your fault — it happens when a culture offers consumption instead of connection. For hooks, the way out begins not with a great feeling but with small practices of love: attention to yourself, honesty, regular care for your body and for those around you. Love, for her, is a verb, not a state; you can start doing it even when it's quiet and empty inside. Sometimes the feeling follows the action rather than preceding it.
emptiness.practice: Do one thing for yourself as you would for someone you love — pour a warm drink, wrap yourself in a blanket — and name it aloud: “This is love.” hooks believed the feeling sometimes follows the action.

confusion.text: The first chapter of bell hooks's main book on love is called “Clarity”: many people are confused about love, she writes, because no one ever really defined it for them. Confusion often arrives the same way — when old words and explanations stop working. Her lesson is that clarity is born through words: naming, distinguishing, defining. In Teaching to Transgress she described education as “the practice of freedom” — a space where you can not know, ask questions and think together without fear of looking foolish. Confusion is not failure but the beginning of thinking. A question asked honestly is already moving you toward understanding, even if the answer doesn't come right away.
confusion.practice: Pick one word surrounded by the most confusion right now — “work,” “home,” “relationship” — and write your own definition, even a rough one. That's how hooks began thinking about love.

fatigue.text: Sisters of the Yam was bell hooks's name for a support group for women used to caring for everyone but themselves — and for a book about the “self-recovery” of those worn out by endless giving. Fatigue is not laziness or a flaw of character: it is a body and soul that have long carried more than they could manage. For hooks, self-care is not selfishness but part of the love ethic: you can't love others sustainably if you treat yourself as a free resource. She also noticed that a culture that prizes productivity makes rest seem suspicious. Your fatigue is a legitimate request for care, and listening to it is also a way of loving.
fatigue.practice: Cancel or postpone one task today and spend the freed half hour doing nothing — lying down, by the window, with tea. Tell yourself aloud: “This is care too.”

boredom.text: The classroom, for bell hooks, should be an exciting place, and boredom in a lesson is not the student's fault but a sign that knowledge has been cut off from life, body and feeling. In life, too, there can be little around you that truly touches you. Her “engaged pedagogy” called for the participation of the whole person, not just the head. Boredom in life is like a boring lesson: we play our roles without asking what actually interests us. Boredom is worth listening to rather than drowning out — it may be calling you toward curiosity, a lively conversation, something that touches you personally.
boredom.practice: Ask someone nearby — or yourself, out loud — a question whose answer you truly want: “What's really on your mind these days?” Engaged pedagogy begins with a living question.

joy.text: A shared meal, a conversation late into the night, a classroom where learning suddenly came alive — bell hooks treasured such moments and wrote that love is not only work and responsibility but also pleasure, lightness, laughter. Your joy is a celebration, and it needs no justification. Her classrooms often rang with laughter: hooks believed laughter doesn't hinder thought but frees it. For people who have lived through hardship, joy for hooks is also an affirmation of their own humanity: the capacity to delight in life even when the world is pressing down. Joy doesn't cancel seriousness or make you frivolous; it feeds the strength for love and care. Let yourself notice it fully, in all its details.
joy.practice: Invite someone to share your joy — for tea, a walk, or just a call. hooks believed joy experienced together feeds the strength for love.

love.text: Of all bell hooks's thoughts, one is quoted most often: love is what we do, not only what we feel. If you love right now, this definition may both support and surprise you. Following the psychiatrist M. Scott Peck, hooks defines love as the will to extend oneself for the sake of spiritual growth — one's own or another person's. And following Erich Fromm, she names its ingredients: care, responsibility, respect, knowledge — and adds trust, commitment and honest communication. Such a definition is freeing: to love means not only to feel something strongly but to do what helps you both grow. Your feeling is valuable in itself, and hooks invites you to give it shape in actions.
love.practice: Today do one act from hooks's list — care, respect, attention or trust — for someone close or for yourself, and silently call it by its name: love.

quote.text: The will to extend one's self for the purpose of nurturing one's own or another's spiritual growth.
quote.author: M. Scott Peck
quote.source: The Road Less Traveled (1978); bell hooks makes this definition the foundation of All About Love

gratitude.text: The Black women teachers of her segregated Kentucky school taught young Gloria with such devotion that learning felt like a celebration — in Teaching to Transgress bell hooks remembers them with gratitude, as people who saw the future in their students. Gratitude is a warm feeling that reminds us: we don't create ourselves alone. She wrote with the same tenderness about her grandparents, whose house was a refuge for her. For hooks, gratitude is tied to recognition — one of the ingredients of love: to see what another has done for you and to say it out loud. Gratitude is love turned back through time: it connects us to a chain of care that stretches across generations.
gratitude.practice: Say thank you — in person, by phone or in a voice message — to someone who once believed in you. Name out loud what exactly they did for you.

hope.text: The subtitle of one of bell hooks's books is A Pedagogy of Hope: hope, she thought, can be learned the way reading is learned. Hope is the courage to expect good even when the grounds are fragile. For hooks, hope is not passive waiting but a practice: we hope when we keep building connections, learning and caring without seeing any guarantee of the outcome. hooks was inspired by the Brazilian educator Paulo Freire, for whom hope was inseparable from action. Hope is especially needed where it seems nothing is changing — and it holds up better together with others. Your hope is not naive: it is part of the effort by which people in every age have made life better.
hope.practice: This week, do one small thing that builds the future with others: help a neighbour, volunteer for an hour, teach someone something you know.

quote.text: The moment we choose to love we begin to move against domination, against oppression. The moment we choose to love we begin to move towards freedom.
quote.author: bell hooks
quote.source: Outlaw Culture (1994), “Love as the Practice of Freedom”

nostalgia.text: After decades in big cities, bell hooks returned late in life to the hills of her native Kentucky and wrote Belonging: A Culture of Place — a book about the land and people of her childhood. Nostalgia is a longing for the place and time that shaped us, and it has its own tenderness. She didn't idealize the past: there was much pain and injustice in it. But she knew how to recognize what had nourished her — for example, what she called “homeplace”: the home where Black families created a space of dignity and care in a world that denied it to them. Nostalgia needs neither to be rejected nor turned into a cult. You can ask: what exactly from the past do I want to bring with me into the present?
nostalgia.practice: Make a small “homeplace” at home — a corner from the past: set out an old photo, cook a childhood dish, play a song. Let the spirit of the past live in the present.

craving.text: A culture short on love, as bell hooks saw it, sells comfort in packaging: things, food and endless entertainment promise to fill the lack quickly — and without the risk of being rejected. A craving is a strong wave, and being swept up by it doesn't mean you are weak. A craving often points not only to its object but also to what that object is standing in for: rest, closeness, relief, the feeling that you matter to someone. This understanding is not an order to “stop wanting.” It simply places a second question next to the first: what am I actually missing right now? The wave rises and falls; you can wait it out with kindness toward yourself.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, take three slow breaths, as Thich Nhat Hanh, hooks's teacher, taught, and ask yourself: “If this were about a feeling rather than a thing, what feeling would it be?”

addiction.text: A circle of people on folding chairs, where each can tell the truth without judgment — bell hooks saw in such communities an image of healing, and did not see addiction as a moral failure: shame helps little here. bell hooks linked the prevalence of addiction to a culture in which people lack reliable care and in which consumption promises to replace closeness. If love for hooks is always a choice, a will to grow, then addiction gradually takes away precisely a person's freedom to choose; so it is not a matter of strength of character but of an unfreedom anyone can fall into. The way out, for hooks, is not a lonely battle but the restoring of connections: healing, she wrote, almost never happens in isolation. In many mutual-help communities people do exactly this — meet themselves and one another without judgment. You deserve care right now, not only “later.”
addiction.practice: Today, find the contact of one person or mutual-help group where you can talk about your struggle without shame, and save it. You don't need to decide anything now: it's enough to know the circle exists.

hangover.text: bell hooks considered shame a poor teacher: it drives a person into silence and isolation, and isolation usually only makes things heavier. The morning after, your body is heavy, your head holds only fragments, and shame is often standing close by. Her alternative is responsibility without self-abasement, as in Fromm: acknowledging what happened and taking care of the consequences and of yourself. What you need now is not verdicts but care: water, rest, quiet, a warm word. You can work out what happened and why later, when you feel better. Treating yourself kindly on a hard morning doesn't mean approving of everything that happened; it means not abandoning yourself.
hangover.practice: Do for your body what you would do for a dear friend after a hard night: a glass of water, a wash, an open window. Going over yesterday can wait.

euphoria.text: There are moments when an idea suddenly catches fire in a classroom and everyone comes alive at once — bell hooks treasured that excitement and wrote about the joy of conversation and community as an almost bodily experience. A high, when the world shines and everything seems possible, is a wonderful feeling, and you can simply live it. A high is fullest when it is shared: joy experienced together becomes a bridge to others. hooks also valued clarity — not to cool the delight, but so that it doesn't carry you away from the people close to you and from yourself. Enjoy this state and stay connected: tell someone you're feeling good right now.
euphoria.practice: Write down in a word or two what is making you so happy right now, and send those words to one person close to you. Joy, for hooks, is fuller when shared.

crash.text: Commitment was on bell hooks's list of love's ingredients — the readiness to be there not only on the joyful days. The drop after a high can be sharp: yesterday it seemed you could handle anything, today it's hard even to get up — and that doesn't cancel the value of the good that was. You can make the same commitment to yourself — not to abandon yourself when your strength has gone. Instead of demanding the old high from yourself, her love ethic would suggest gentle attention: what do you need right now to get through this day? The swings of feeling don't define you; what remains is your ability to care for yourself at both the high point and the low.
crash.practice: Make a list of three tiny tasks for today, one just for pleasure. Tick each off the way you'd keep a promise to someone you love.

panic.text: Breathing in, “I know I am breathing in”; breathing out, “I know I am breathing out” — bell hooks learned this simple practice from Thich Nhat Hanh. Right now your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems it will always be like this — it really is hard, and you are not exaggerating. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. hooks valued the practice of mindfulness — returning to the present through the body and the breath. She insisted that a person is a unity of mind, body and spirit, not just thoughts. In a moment of panic there is nothing you need to understand or solve. You only need to come back to your body and wait out the wave — the way you would hold the hand of a frightened friend.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and breathe like this: on the in-breath, silently, “I know I'm breathing in”; on the out-breath, “I know I'm breathing out,” making it a little longer. Then name aloud five objects around you.

dread.text: “Dominator culture has tried to keep us all afraid,” bell hooks wrote. A heavy premonition that something bad is about to happen is exhausting, and you don't have to be ashamed of it or force it away. bell hooks wrote that fear makes us hide and separate from others — and it is in isolation that it grows. She didn't promise that the world is safe: she knew well how much cruelty is in it. But she found support in connection — in people with whom you can share the load, and in practices of mindfulness that bring you back to the present. A premonition speaks of the future, but we can only live now — and right now you are here, you are breathing. For today, it is enough to live through today.
dread.practice: Go outside for five minutes and walk slowly, noticing with each step: “I am here. I am breathing.” The future can wait; right now there is only this step.

fomo.text: Consumer culture, as bell hooks saw it, turns happiness into a shop window and teaches us to compare our lives with pictures made to sell. The feeling that life is happening somewhere else, to other people, grows especially strong when we constantly see others' hand-picked moments. Advertising, in her view, sells not things but a dream of a life we supposedly lack. The fear of missing out is largely a product of that shop window, not accurate knowledge of what you lack. Her love ethic suggests looking not wider but deeper: what in your own life is already waiting for attention and care — a friendship, an activity, a place? Fullness, for hooks, comes not from the quantity of experiences but from presence and connection.
fomo.practice: Put your phone in another room for half an hour and spend that time with what is already in your life: call a friend, water the plants, read. hooks called fullness presence, not quantity.

sleepless.text: In the community of Thich Nhat Hanh, from whom bell hooks learned, a mindfulness bell is rung so that everyone stops for a moment and returns to the breath. A sleepless night can be very lonely: the world is asleep and your thoughts keep circling — and you are not doing anything “wrong.” Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's tradition of mindfulness, bell hooks spoke of the wholeness of body, mind and spirit — and of how caring for yourself means listening to your body rather than giving it orders. At night the mind tends to exaggerate what is hard, so right now you don't need to solve a single question. You can simply treat yourself like a loved one who can't fall asleep: gently, without reproach, without hurry. Rest is not only sleep; lying quietly in the dark also restores you little by little.
sleepless.practice: Imagine the soft sound of a bell and, at its sound, take three slow breaths out with your palm on your chest. Tell yourself: “Nothing needs to be decided right now.”

betrayal.text: For bell hooks, trust is not a pleasant extra in love but its foundation: without it, the house stands on sand. Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it strikes at the very ground the relationship stood on — and that pain is real. In All About Love bell hooks calls trust and honesty essential ingredients of love, and lying one of the main reasons love is so fragile in our culture. She noticed that many people are taught from childhood to lie for convenience and to “keep the peace in the family,” and this habit later destroys intimacy. Betrayal is not proof of your naivety but a violation for which the one who committed it is responsible. Your capacity to trust is not a weakness but something of value, worth protecting.
betrayal.practice: Tell one person you trust what happened, and end with: “I wasn't naive — I trusted.” hooks considered the ability to trust something worth protecting.

jealousy.text: Culture, bell hooks wrote, teaches us from childhood to confuse love with possession — as if loving meant owning and controlling a person. Jealousy grips the heart with the fear of losing someone dear, and that old lesson is easy to recognize in its grip. Love and control, hooks insisted, don't live well under one roof. For hooks, love rests on respect and mutuality — on recognizing the other's freedom. Jealousy often speaks less about the other person than about our own insecurity — the fear that we are not enough, and a lack of trust. This is not a verdict but an invitation: to notice your vulnerability and take care of it, instead of demanding guarantees from the other.
jealousy.practice: Make one gesture today of respect for your loved one's freedom: don't check, don't ask more than you need, wish them a good evening wherever they are. Notice what happens to your fear.

resentment.text: bell hooks had things to forgive — and she wrote honestly about how long that takes. A grudge that won't let go for years is heavy, and it almost always has a reason: you really were hurt. In All About Love bell hooks wrote about forgiveness as a gift we give first of all to ourselves, to free ourselves from the power of the past. But forgiveness, for her, doesn't mean forgetting or excusing: you can acknowledge that you were treated unjustly and still consider it unjust. Forgiveness is a process, not a duty, and it can't be forced. Resentment keeps the memory of the wound, and first it needs to be heard. Only pain that has been acknowledged can, over time, loosen its grip.
resentment.practice: Write a letter you won't send: what you'd like this person to understand about your pain. hooks believed acknowledged pain loosens its grip over time.

heartbreak.text: In Communion bell hooks gathers the stories of women who, after breakups, learned to love all over again. A broken heart hurts with your whole body, and there is nothing shameful in that. bell hooks wrote that many of us learned about love in places where it was mixed with pain, and so a breakup often touches not only the present loss but old wounds too. At the same time her view offers support: if love is action and choice, then the capacity to love doesn't leave along with the person. It stays in you — in your care, your openness, your ability to trust — and you can direct it toward yourself and others. hooks insisted that we heal together: friends, loved ones, community can hold you while your heart mends. The strength of the pain is a sign of how deeply you are able to attach.
heartbreak.practice: Call someone who knows how to listen and say honestly: “I'm having a hard time right now.” You don't need to explain more — hooks believed hearts heal in community.

quote.text: Rarely, if ever, are any of us healed in isolation. Healing is an act of communion.
quote.author: bell hooks

impostor.text: A young woman from a working-class Southern family at Stanford — bell hooks knew well what it was like to sit among people with different manners, language and confidence; she wrote about it in Teaching to Transgress and Where We Stand: Class Matters. The feeling that you're here by accident and about to be “found out” is very common, especially among those who have come to a new environment from far away. hooks came to understand that this feeling was not proof of her inadequacy but a consequence of the rules of the game having been set by others. Your “impostor” feeling often speaks of the distance you have traveled, not of a shortcoming. And the experience of a person “from the margins” is valuable: hooks called the margin a space of “radical openness.”
impostor.practice: Write down three things you can do or understand precisely because of your path. hooks called the margin a space of “radical openness” — this is your wealth, not a shortcoming.

self_hatred.text: Rock My Soul (2003) is a book bell hooks devoted entirely to self-esteem — the thing so many people lack. When an inner voice keeps saying that you are bad, unwanted, unworthy, it hurts a great deal — and that voice is not telling the truth about you. bell hooks wrote that many people absorb in childhood the shaming and neglect they experienced from adults and later repeat them to themselves; this is not your nature but something learned. In All About Love and Rock My Soul she called self-love the foundation of all love and wrote about practices of self-esteem, among them self-acceptance: the decision to be on your own side even before the feeling has arrived. For hooks, love is action: you can treat yourself gently even without believing you deserve it. You do deserve it.
self_hatred.practice: Say aloud to yourself the sentence you would say to a friend who spoke about themselves in these words. hooks called this deciding to be on your own side before the feeling arrives.

helplessness.text: Growing up in a segregated town, bell hooks saw people with no power at all doing small things that kept their dignity intact. Helplessness is a heavy feeling: it seems nothing depends on you. Sometimes that is partly true: there are circumstances one person can't change. bell hooks knew well the power of large systems — racism, poverty, patriarchy — and never blamed people for being unable to defeat them alone. But she wrote about the move “from object to subject”: from being someone things are done to, to being someone who speaks and acts, however modestly. Her image of “homeplace” speaks to the same thing: people deprived of power in society created spaces of dignity and care at home. When the big things are beyond your power, the small ones are still yours.
helplessness.practice: Draw two circles: in the big one, what doesn't depend on you right now; in the small one, one thing that does. Do that one thing today.

procrastination.text: The author of more than thirty books, bell hooks insisted in Remembered Rapture that writing is a practice you learn, not a gift for the chosen few. Putting things off is not laziness: more often fear hides behind it — of not coping, of being judged, of seeing the gap between the idea and the result. Mistakes, for her, were part of the craft, not a cause for shame. In Teaching to Transgress she criticized an education in which mistakes are shamed and in which learning therefore becomes frightening. If fear of judgment lies behind your procrastination, what helps is not pressure but a kinder environment — including an inner one. Give yourself the right to an imperfect first step: a draft is not a verdict, but a beginning.
procrastination.practice: In five minutes, do the tiniest “wrong” version of the first step — a clumsy sketch, one line, a call without preparation. hooks called a draft a beginning, not a verdict.

uprooted.text: California, Connecticut, Ohio, New York — for decades bell hooks lived far from the Kentucky hills, and in Belonging: A Culture of Place she described how she longed for them and eventually returned. The sense of being cut off from your roots is vivid and heavy: you can live in a new place for years and still not feel at home. But the main thing she shows is that belonging is not only a point on a map; it is a practice of connection with land, people and memory. Roots can not only be lost but also grown — by strengthening the threads to the past and making new ones where you are now. Your longing shows how much belonging matters to you.
uprooted.practice: Take a slow walk around your new place today, the way hooks walked her hills, and find one tree, bench or corner you'd like to come back to. Roots can be grown here too.

overload.text: A well from which to draw strength for love — that is how bell hooks thought of silence, contemplation and spiritual practice. When there's too much of everything — tasks, news, other people's expectations — it's hard even to think, and that is not a personal failure. bell hooks wrote that a culture of domination and consumption encourages endless busyness and places almost no value on silence, contemplation, rest. Spiritual life — for her not necessarily religion, but a practice of inner quiet and attention — was a source of clarity and of the strength to love. Overload takes away our ability to be attentive to ourselves and to others, and so our ability to love. Protecting your time and your quiet is care, not selfishness.
overload.practice: Choose one task you can skip today and spend the freed ten minutes in complete silence — no screen, no music. That isn't laziness; it's the well.

unreality.text: In Teaching to Transgress bell hooks argues against the habit of splitting a person into head and body — as if thinking happened somewhere apart from the living, feeling self. The feeling that the world, or you yourself, has become unreal, as if behind glass, is frightening and disorienting; hooks didn't write about it directly, but her idea of wholeness helps speak of it calmly. We are, for hooks, body, mind and spirit all at once. When reality seems to recede, what gently helps is returning to bodily presence and to other people — to what is warm, tangible, simple. This feeling comes in waves, and it doesn't make you any less real.
unreality.practice: Hold something warm in your hands — a cup, a loved one's hand, a pet — and describe aloud what you feel. Then name the place where you are.

awe.text: The Kentucky hills where bell hooks grew up taught her a sense of connection with all living things, and she considered spirituality an important part of the love ethic. Awe is a rare feeling, when the world suddenly turns out to be bigger than we thought and everything inside goes quiet. For her this was not sentimentality but part of an ethic: whoever feels connected to all living things finds it harder to dominate. In Belonging the land appears as something that restores both humility and joy. Awe is the moment when hierarchies and competition recede and we feel part of a larger whole. You don't need to do anything with it — only let it be and perhaps remember how it feels in your body.
awe.practice: Be silent for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, your palm on your heart. hooks would say hierarchies recede in such moments — simply be part of something larger.

relief.text: You only really feel the backpack you've carried all day once you take it off — bell hooks knew this oddity well. Relief is like finally being able to breathe out, and it deserves attention. bell hooks wrote that many people become so used to constant pressure that they take it for normal. It is the moment of relief that reveals how hard things were — and it is a good time for self-care: to acknowledge that you've been through something difficult and let your body rest. Relief can also hint at what exactly was so heavy, so that you can notice it sooner in the future. Just let yourself enjoy the lightness — without rushing to the next task.
relief.practice: Celebrate the relief with a small ritual: a long exhale, shoes off, your favourite tea — and say aloud: “I made it through.”

calm.text: A “Buddhist Christian” is what bell hooks called herself, and from Thich Nhat Hanh she learned mindfulness — the art of being fully in the present. Calm is a precious state, and it's good simply to feel it fully. She called spiritual practices — meditation, prayer, silence — a source from which to draw strength for love and for work in the world. Calm is not detachment but a foundation: from it, it's easier to listen, understand and respond to others with care rather than with a jolt. In a culture that prizes haste such minutes are easy to dismiss as useless, but for hooks they are part of caring for yourself, not its opposite. Stay in it; nothing needs to be added.
calm.practice: Move your attention from the top of your head to your feet and find three places in your body that feel calm right now. Remember them — hooks considered such minutes part of self-care.

inspiration.text: At nineteen, while still a student, bell hooks began writing her first book, Ain't I a Woman. Inspiration is the excitement of an idea coming alive and making you want to act. bell hooks knew it well: she wrote about the “excitement” in a classroom when teacher and students discover something new together, and considered this feeling a legitimate part of thinking rather than an obstacle to it. For her, learning and creating meant taking part as a whole person — with your body, your feelings, your life experience. Inspiration grows in dialogue: you want to share it, and sharing makes it stronger. Let it be, write your ideas down while they're hot, and don't rush to judge them: criticism can wait, and living excitement is easily scared off.
inspiration.practice: Tell someone your idea in its raw form — over tea, in a voice message — and ask them not to judge but to ask one question. hooks believed thought grows stronger in dialogue.

quote.text: The classroom remains the most radical space of possibility in the academy.
quote.author: bell hooks
quote.source: Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom (1994)

schadenfreude.text: Who's above, who's below, who won, who lost — this, for bell hooks, is how “dominator culture” teaches us to see people. Secret pleasure at someone else's failure brings shame, but feeling it doesn't make you a bad person. Even love and friendship turn into competition in such a culture. In that picture, someone else's fall feels like your own rise. Schadenfreude often speaks of an old hurt, or of times when you yourself felt humiliated and unrecognized. The love ethic doesn't shame you for this feeling; it invites you to ask: which wound of mine just responded? When a wound is noticed, the wish for someone else to suffer usually loses its force.
schadenfreude.practice: Put a hand on your heart and ask yourself: which wound of mine just responded — where was I not recognized? Name it silently with the kindness you'd offer someone else's.

contempt.text: Sticking on a label is faster than looking at a person — bell hooks saw this as one of the main lessons a hierarchical society teaches. Contempt is a cold feeling: it places the other beneath you. Sometimes it arises as a defense — when we have been hurt, or when someone has behaved truly badly. bell hooks saw clearly how society teaches contempt — for the poor, for women, for those who are “different” — and how contempt props up hierarchies. Her love ethic is built on respect, one of the ingredients of love in Erich Fromm: seeing the other as they are, not through a label. This doesn't mean approving of what others do. Contempt often protects us from pain or from the fear of turning out to be like the person we despise. It's worth asking what exactly it is covering up.
contempt.practice: Picture this person as a child — about seven, in a schoolyard. What do you see without the label? For hooks, respect begins with seeing, not with approving.

disgust.text: Advertising, films, schoolyard jokes — bell hooks showed how culture teaches disgust toward certain bodies and groups of people, and how this learned feeling sustains injustice. Disgust is a strong bodily reaction — you want to turn away, pull back — and it can be aimed at a situation, at people, sometimes at yourself. But there is also disgust that honestly reports, “this is unacceptable to me” — and it deserves respect as a boundary. It matters to tell where your disgust comes from — from your own values or from other people's judgments you have absorbed. If it is aimed at yourself, it's worth asking whose words you are hearing. Perhaps you were simply taught to look at yourself that way.
disgust.practice: Take a step back and three calm breaths, then ask: is this disgust protecting something I value, or repeating someone else's judgment? Answer aloud in one word: “mine” or “theirs.”

revenge.text: For bell hooks, justice and returning pain are different roads, even if they start from the same wound: she didn't deny anger at injustice, but she clearly told the pursuit of justice apart from the urge to hurt back. The wish for revenge usually arises where there was real pain, and behind it is a need for your wound to be acknowledged. Her love ethic starts from the view that violence and domination, even in retaliation, continue the very cycle we want to leave. Revenge promises to restore dignity, but dignity is restored more through acknowledgment, support and the protection of your boundaries. The feeling can be lived through fully — in words, on paper, in conversation with someone who understands — without turning it into an act against anyone.
revenge.practice: Write down what exactly the person who hurt you would need to understand or acknowledge. Read it aloud to someone on your side — acknowledgment can come that way too.

anger_at_loved.text: bell hooks grew up in a family of seven children and knew that love is not a constant warm feeling but a practice of care, respect and responsibility, with room for difficult emotions too. Anger at those closest to you — a partner, parents, children — is very common, and so is shame about it; being angry with the people you love doesn't mean loving them less. At the same time hooks stressed that where there is love there is no place for abuse and humiliation — and this applies to how we express anger. Anger at someone close often points to an unmet need — for rest, respect, help — and to the fact that it hasn't yet been spoken about. The task is not to stop being angry but to find words and a safe form for the anger.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, pause for three breaths and begin your sentence with “I need…” instead of “You always…” You can first say it aloud when you're alone.

ambivalence.text: In her memoirs Bone Black and Wounds of Passion, bell hooks writes openly about her family — about people she loved who also caused her pain. Loving and being unable to stand the same person at once is not hypocrisy but the truth of many close relationships. hooks showed that care and hurt can be joined in a relationship, and that acknowledging both doesn't destroy love but makes it more honest. For hooks, love is a choice and an action, not a demand to feel only warm feelings. You don't have to choose one feeling and cancel the other. You can hold them together and ask yourself which actions match your values.
ambivalence.practice: Picture a patchwork quilt like the ones hooks's grandmother sewed: light and dark patches side by side. Silently name three “patches” of this relationship — warm and hard — without throwing any away.

guilty_relief.text: Care and responsibility were written into the very definition of love for bell hooks — and she knew how heavy they become when they last for years. Relief after a breakup, leaving a job or even the death of a seriously ill loved one often comes with shame, but relief and love don't contradict each other. Love, for her, never meant endless self-sacrifice: care for yourself was part of it on equal terms. Relief often shows how much strength you were giving. For hooks, loss is part of love, and grief weaves together all kinds of feelings. Relief doesn't cancel your attachment; it honestly marks the end of strain. Allow yourself to feel both, without choosing the “right” one.
guilty_relief.practice: Write one sentence: “I feel relieved, and at the same time I…” — and finish it with whatever is also true. hooks believed grief weaves all kinds of feelings together.

indifference.text: “Boys don't cry” — in The Will to Change bell hooks shows how this lesson teaches many people from childhood to switch off their feelings in order to survive where vulnerability is dangerous; she called it emotional numbness. Sometimes, where something “should” move you, everything inside is quiet — and that feels unsettling. Such switching off is a defense, not heartlessness. Indifference sometimes appears when there are too many feelings or they are too painful. The love ethic doesn't demand that you immediately feel the “right” thing; it offers patient attention — feelings come back when it becomes safe enough. The fact that you notice your indifference and are worried about it already speaks of living care.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself the way you'd ask a frightened child: “If a feeling is hiding under this quiet, what is it?” Don't demand an answer — hooks believed feelings return when it becomes safe.

escape.text: Yale, Oberlin, New York — and finally the small Berea College in her native Kentucky: bell hooks changed her life more than once and left prestigious positions. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and go where no one knows you says that your present life has become too cramped. But she described change as a choice grounded in values, not as running away from pain. The dream of escape hints at what you are missing — freedom, rest, meaning, community. It is worth listening to without rushing to tear anything down. Sometimes a small change is enough to make it easier to breathe; sometimes the dream gradually turns into a well-considered plan.
escape.practice: Make one small change today grounded in a value rather than in running away: take a new route, drop one “should” for one “want,” spend an hour where you breathe more freely.

forbidden_attraction.text: In Communion and All About Love, bell hooks separates three things we tend to blur: attraction, infatuation and love. An attraction to someone you “mustn't” be attracted to can be confusing and frightening, but the feeling itself doesn't make you bad: desire doesn't ask permission. Infatuation, she wrote, often rests on fantasy and projection — we see in the other what we lack, and that is not yet knowing the person. Love, by contrast, requires knowledge, time and mutuality. Such an attraction can tell you a lot about yourself — about a longing for aliveness, attention, freedom. You can explore it calmly, without rushing to conclusions about yourself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Silently name three things you actually know about this person and three you may have filled in yourself. hooks believed love begins with knowledge, not projection.

social_anxiety.text: Young Gloria was punished for “talking back” to adults — and bell hooks later titled a book Talking Back and wrote about speaking in your own voice as an act of courage. Fear of people and their judgment can turn a simple meeting into an ordeal, and nothing is wrong with you for it. For a girl from Kentucky it was a long road — from a pupil who was hushed to a lecturer heard by thousands. In Teaching to Transgress she strove for a classroom where every voice is valued and no one fears ridicule. Fear of judgment grows where we were measured and shamed, and weakens in spaces of respect. Such spaces can be sought out — starting small.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, say one sentence aloud in your ordinary voice — “Good to see you,” say — just to hear it. A voice that has already sounded today is easier to raise among people.

uncertainty.text: Education as “the practice of freedom” — bell hooks made Paulo Freire's formula her own: to learn is to enter a place where there are no ready-made answers, and freedom always involves risk. Freire taught adult peasants to read starting from the words that mattered to them, and hooks admired his faith that learning is possible in any circumstances. Uncertainty is draining: it's hard to plan and hard to relax when you don't know what will happen. hooks didn't promise guarantees and didn't believe life can be fully controlled. Uncertainty is not only a threat but also a space of possibility, where not everything has been decided for you yet. This doesn't cancel the anxiety, but it gives it neighbors — curiosity and hope.
uncertainty.practice: Ask yourself two questions aloud, like a good teacher: “What do I know for sure today?” and “What could I learn here?” Answer at least the first.

waiting.text: Love, for bell hooks, is a patient practice: commitment, one of its ingredients, shows itself over time, not in a single moment. Waiting — for results, a reply, news — stretches time and keeps you suspended, and it is hard. Thich Nhat Hanh, from whom she learned, taught that even washing the dishes can be meditation. While waiting we often live entirely in the future, and the present is left without attention. This practice of mindfulness brings you back to what is happening now: to your breath, to the person beside you, to the task in your hands. Waiting doesn't have to be empty time — it can become a time of caring for yourself while the answer is still on its way.
waiting.practice: While you wait, do one thing slowly, as Thich Nhat Hanh taught: wash a cup, feeling the warm water, or take ten steps, feeling your feet. Waiting can be a time of care too.

regret.text: A scar remembers the wound without hurting the way it did — bell hooks taught us to look at the past in a similar way. Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. It shows that you care how your life turns out, and it speaks of values that may now be clearer to you. bell hooks wrote that love requires honesty, above all with yourself: looking at the past without embellishment and without cruelty. For her, responsibility is not endless guilt but the ability to learn from experience and act differently. Regret is knowledge you didn't have back then. You can't carry it into the past, but you can bring it into the present — into how you live, love and choose today. Back then you were who you were able to be.
regret.practice: Write: “Back then I didn't know…, and now I know…” — and pick one situation this week where that knowledge will be useful.

longing.text: Love, for bell hooks, is what we do, so it doesn't vanish when a person is far away: care, memory and gratitude go on living in us and in our actions. When you miss a particular person, it is love looking for somewhere to go — quiet or sharp, but always about a bond that matters to you. hooks also insisted that one person shouldn't be your only source of warmth: we need circles of community, friends, people with whom to share life. Longing is a sign of your ability to attach, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. You can hold it gently while staying open to other connections too.
longing.practice: Write this person a letter — whether to send it you can decide later. Tell them what you remember and what you're grateful for: that is love as action.

world_pain.text: bell hooks's “love ethic” doesn't stop at the front door: in her view it should also guide how people treat one another across the world. Pain for the world — from news of war, cruelty, injustice — shows that your heart hasn't closed, but carrying it alone is almost impossible. hooks also knew that despair is depleting, and she found support in community and spiritual practice. You don't need to absorb all the pain of the world to prove your sensitivity. You can choose how much news to take in, look after yourself, and do something small and concrete where you are.
world_pain.practice: Limit the news to one window of time today, then do one small kind thing nearby — for a neighbour, a colleague, a stranger. The love ethic begins where you stand.

rejection.text: “Be good, easy, successful — and you'll be loved”: bell hooks wrote that many of us absorb this condition in childhood. Rejection — when you weren't chosen, accepted, wanted — hurts, and this pain is very ancient. She knew this firsthand: a childhood in which approval had to be earned left a long mark on her. That's why a refusal so easily sounds like a verdict on the whole person. But for hooks, love begins with self-love — with self-esteem that doesn't depend on other people's approval. Rejection speaks of the other's decision, limitations or tastes, of a mismatch, not of your worth. It hurts because you opened up — and that openness remains your strength.
rejection.practice: Do one act of self-love today that depends on no one else's decision: cook a favourite meal, go somewhere you feel good. Name it aloud: “This is for me.”

abandonment.text: Her grandparents' house in Kentucky was a place young Gloria could always run to and be expected — bell hooks would later call such places homeplace. The fear of being abandoned can run very deep: it makes you cling, check, and panic at any sign of coolness. It is often rooted in early experience, when care was unreliable. bell hooks wrote that many people grew up in families where love was mixed with unpredictability, and later carry that expectation into adult relationships. None of this is your fault. For hooks, an important part of healing is learning to give yourself the reliability that was once missing, and building relationships on trust and honest communication. Your fear is the trace of an old wound, not a prophecy. Today you have the chance to care for yourself and to seek out people who stay.
abandonment.practice: Think of someone who stayed even though you feared they wouldn't, and send them a few warm words. Let that be your small homeplace — a place where you're expected.

unrequited.text: Infatuation, bell hooks wrote, often rests on a fantasy about the other, while love requires mutuality — knowledge, trust and commitment on both sides. A feeling with nowhere to return to hurts especially sharply, but it is no less real for that. For hooks this distinction is not cold classification but a way to treat your own heart more gently. Unrequited love is a genuine capacity to love that hasn't yet found a mutual space, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. But hooks also reminded us that love is care for growth, including your own: sometimes loving yourself means ceasing to wait for an answer where there is none, and directing your warmth to where it can be received.
unrequited.practice: Today, send some of this warmth where it can be received: call a friend, help someone, do something kind for yourself. hooks called love care for growth — including your own.

humiliation.text: In the school bell hooks was moved to after desegregation, Black children were met with mockery and coldness — she knew what it is like when someone tries to strip your dignity in front of others. Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences, and if someone treated you this way, the responsibility lies with the one who humiliated you. bell hooks wrote that humiliation and shaming often serve as tools of power — in families, schools, workplaces — and have nothing to do with love or care. Her love ethic is based on recognition: seeing in everyone a person worthy of respect. Your dignity is not defined by how you were treated; it can be wounded but not taken away. Healing begins when you can tell what you went through to people who respect you.
humiliation.practice: Read aloud to yourself the sentence you'd want to hear from someone on your side: “You didn't deserve that. Your dignity is still yours.” Say it once more, slower.

quote.text: Abuse and neglect negate love. Care and affirmation, the opposite of abuse and humiliation, are the foundation of love.
quote.author: bell hooks

body_shame.text: In 1999 bell hooks published a children's book, Happy to Be Nappy — a celebration of the hair Black girls were taught to be ashamed of. If you're unhappy with your body, that unhappiness rarely arises on its own. In Feminism Is for Everybody bell hooks devoted a chapter to beauty: she showed how culture and advertising impose narrow standards of appearance, especially on women, and how people begin to look at themselves through someone else's eyes. In Black Looks she wrote about how media images teach people to be ashamed of their looks, their skin color, their features. Your shame about your body is largely learned, not deserved. Self-love, for hooks, includes caring for your body as a home rather than as a project to be fixed. You can treat it gently already now.
body_shame.practice: Do one thing for your body as for a home you love: rub cream into your hands, brush your hair slowly, wrap up warm. Thank it for what it did for you today.

illness.text: Her central idea — love is care — is tested precisely at the bedside, though bell hooks wrote little about illness directly. When your body lets you down, your usual sense of yourself collapses — plans, strength, independence — and fear, anger or sadness are entirely fitting. hooks criticized a culture that ranks independence and productivity so highly that asking for help seems like weakness. Interdependence is not a failure but part of human life, since each of us at some point needs the care of others. Illness does not lessen your worth. Letting others care for you is also a way of taking part in love, and gentleness toward yourself now is not a whim but a necessity.
illness.practice: Ask one person today for one specific kind of help — briefly, without apologising. hooks believed letting yourself be cared for is also a way of taking part in love.

pride.text: A girl from a working-class family in Hopkinsville, Kentucky, became a professor and the author of more than thirty books — bell hooks knew the cost of such a path. Pride in what you have done is a healthy, well-earned feeling, and you can enjoy it. hooks called self-esteem the foundation of self-love: acknowledging your work, your growth, your strengths. At the same time, for hooks pride is fullest when it is seen and shared: one person's success almost always rests on the support of many — teachers, family, community. Being proud of yourself is not immodest; it is a form of recognition, and recognition is one of the ingredients of love. Name what you have done, and those who helped you along the way.
pride.practice: Tell someone, in a full sentence, what you're proud of — and name one person who helped along the way. hooks considered recognition one of love's ingredients.

melancholy.text: One of bell hooks's last books is Appalachian Elegy, poems about her native hills. Bright sadness, where sorrow meets tenderness, sounds like such an elegy, and you don't have to do anything with it. bell hooks loved poetry and wrote poems herself; writing was for her a space where deep feelings could be lived through and reflected on. In Belonging she describes with tenderness and sadness her native hills, loved ones who are gone, a vanished way of life — and this sadness doesn't break her but connects her with what she loved. Melancholy is a way of remembering and cherishing. It doesn't need fixing — only space and, perhaps, words.
melancholy.practice: Write a few lines about what brings on this bright sadness — not a report, but a small elegy, as hooks did.
